idiom_name: one parsing function per syntax node over a token stream (SwiftParser shape)
implementation_notes: Swift's own toolchain is the model: swift-syntax's SwiftParser implements a recursive descent parser whose documentation states that there is a one-to-one correspondence between syntax nodes and parsing functions, with token consumption split between unconditional consumeAnyToken and conditional at(_:where:)/eat(_:), and expect(_:) synthesising missing tokens so the tree stays well-formed on invalid input. In application code: an enum of token kinds with associated values, a Parser struct holding the token array and an index, one function per rule returning AST nodes, and throws or a Result type for errors, with pattern matching and optional chaining for alternatives. Nothing in the standard library replaces the structure; reuse SwiftParser when the input is Swift source and hand-write only for grammars you own.
pitfalls: Swift has no tail-call guarantee and a fixed stack: deeply nested input must be rejected by an explicit depth counter, because a stack overflow traps the process instead of throwing.
eat/expect mutating the cursor while returning tokens is easy to get wrong with defer; keep all mutation in one place and never expose the raw index to rule bodies.
Enums with associated values are value types: recursive ASTs need indirect cases or a class/box, otherwise the compiler rejects the type as infinitely sized.
